text.p: President Clinton Sunday expressed optimism that the Teamsters union and United Parcel Service would settle their dispute to end a two-week strike against the nation's largest package delivery company.
"It's my gut feeling they'll settle," he told reporters as he arrived at Martha's Vineyard for a three-week vacation. "They're that close," he said, holding up two fingers not very far apart.
"It's a good deal. It will set a precedent for unions," Clinton said.

Earlier Sunday, Teamsters President Ron Carey said on NBC television that marathon talks with UPS had made progress for the first time since negotiators hunkered down in a Washington hotel at the request of Labor Secretary Alexis Herman on Thursday morning.

Deputy White House counsel Bruce Lindsey told reporters traveling with Clinton that he believed the two sides would either reach a settlement on Sunday or break off negotiations. He said that if the parties could not reach agreement tonight Herman would call for a recess in the talks to allow negotiators to get some rest.
The two sides have been in meetings since Thursday morning, taking a few brief sleep breaks along the way.

The walkout by drivers, loaders and sorters on Aug. 4 has crippled the nation's largest package delivery firm, costing it an estimated $300 million a week in lost revenues and more than a half-billion dollars so far.
